transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05 16:00 UTC | Duration: 46m | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jared Kim (Redwood SE), Leah Morgan (Kairos Head of Platform), Omar Reyes (Kairos SRE), Priya Singh (Dir ML), Ethan Cho (Product)

[00:00:05] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. should we do quick intros then jump to what you're trying to solve?
[00:00:12] Leah: yeah, sounds good. i'm leah, lead platform at kairos. basically we're building an internal assistant + customer facing chat, need to decide hosting and get p95s under control.
[00:00:25] Omar: hi, i'm omar, sre. our objective is predictable latency at scale. we've seen big variance during token bursts.
[00:00:31] Priya: priya here, director of ml. biggest ask: maintain model quality while lowering per-token cost. curious about quantization effects and also routing between variants.
[00:00:39] Maya: awesome. jared and i will cover latency/econ tradeoffs and the profiling plan. quick qualification: what load shapes do you see? avg vs peak?
[00:00:52] Leah: avg is small, maybe 20–30 concurrent sessions, but bursts hit like 2k concurrent users for short windows, 10–30s bursts. typical request is chat snippets, 20–60 tokens response for customer assistant, but internal agent workflows can be 200+ tokens.
[00:01:12] Jared: ok so two distinct patterns — short streaming chat and longer batch-style completions. what's your p95 SLO target for the customer-facing flow?
[00:01:21] Leah: we want p95 under 200ms ideally for the short flows. for internal ML ops longer tails are ok, but cost becomes sensitive.
[00:01:30] Ethan: to add, we may need streaming with partial tokens for progressive UI. can't have 800ms p95 for the UX.
[00:01:37] Maya: makes sense. are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private? any policy or residency constraints?
[00:01:44] Omar: residency on EU data centers for some customer data, plus audit logs and SSO integration requirements. enterprise buyers also ask for dedicated capacity and auditability.
[00:01:55] Priya: plus we want to run some evals ourselves and test quantized variants — might prefer Dedicated or Private to get kernel-level latency control.
[00:02:05] Jared: noted. quick note — Redwood Hosted often gives fastest path to market and seamless autoscaling, but Dedicated can hit tighter p95s with predictable throughput and private networks reduce egress variability. Private adds more ops overhead.
[00:02:21] Leah: can you quantify p95 differences? ballpark numbers for similar workloads?
[00:02:27] Jared: ballpark: for short streaming chat on a modern open model 7B-class with continuous streaming and prefix caching, hosted median can be ~40–60ms per token and p95 around 180–300ms depending on multiplexing and infra. Dedicated can tighten p95 to ~120–180ms by reducing noisy neighbors and pinning GPUs. but long sequences change that.
[00:02:50] Omar: that wide range worries me. what about token/sec and concurrency? we need 2k concurrent sessions, how do we size?
[00:02:58] Maya: we'll run token/sec profiling — we look at effective tokens/s per GPU for your model variant, then factor in average tokens per request, multiplexing factor, and desired p95. we'll share a sizing sheet.
[00:03:09] Jared: important nuance — streaming semantics mean you care about per-token latency, not just throughput. batching helps throughput but increases first-token latency. continuous batching with small batch limits can help.
[00:03:21] Priya: how does KV cache help for short chat? most of our sessions reuse context across turns.
[00:03:27] Jared: KV cache can massively reduce compute for later turns; if you have persistent sessions and reuse tokens, effective tokens/sec per GPU improves and p95 for subsequent tokens drops because only new tokens are generated. caching also interacts with memory footprint — quantization affects that.
[00:03:40] Leah: curious about fallbacks. if Dedicated is saturated, can Redwood route to hosted variants?
[00:03:46] Maya: yes, smart routing can failover to hosted-compatible model variants; we discussed policy-based fallbacks — cost-tiered or latency-tiered. we can configure automatic fallback for peak bursts.
[00:03:58] Omar: we need to ensure data doesn't leak to hosted if some requests must stay in private. can routing respect per-call policies?
[00:04:04] Jared: yes, routing is tag-aware. we can mark invocation metadata to keep specific requests on private/dedicated. for sensitive payloads we can set a hard pin to private.
[00:04:12] Ethan: security question: we need Keystore / KMS integration and audit logs — do you support customer-managed keys and consistent audit exports?
[00:04:19] Maya: yes — Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM integration; Dedicated supports KMS via VPC peering and audit logs have export hooks. we'll send the whitepaper.
[00:04:29] Priya: okay back to performance — can we run a quick scenario on sizing? say 2k concurrent short chat sessions at 25 tokens per response average, streaming enabled, target p95 180ms. what does that imply?
[00:04:41] Jared: rough calc: if each response averages 25 tokens and you want per-token latency to be ~7–10ms to hit that overall, you'd need aggregate token/sec capacity of ~ (2000 sessions * 25 tokens) / avg response window seconds. but sessions are bursty — more meaningful is tokens/sec during peak windows. let's assume bursts of 30s where 2k users each send one request — that's 50k tokens over 30s => ~1.7k tokens/sec sustained for that window. GPU tokens/sec for a 7B quantized model might be 6k–10k tokens/sec depending on kernel and batching. so single GPU could handle that steady tokens/sec but p95 depends on multiplexing and batching behavior.
[00:05:18] Leah: so might we actually run in hosted until we need guaranteed p95?
[00:05:21] Maya: that's common — start hosted for rapid onboarding, run profiling, then migrate to Dedicated if p95 or residency needs arise.
[00:05:28] Omar: i'm worried about cold-starts and scaling during sudden spikes. what are warmup strategies?
[00:05:33] Jared: we support pre-warming pools, burst capacity, and graceful autoscale. plus cache priming using historical prefixes. cold-starts can add hundreds of ms if a GPU needs to load model weights and compile kernels. Dedicated reduces that by keeping reserved pools.
[00:05:48] Priya: any guidance on quantization regressions? quality vs perf tradeoffs?
[00:05:53] Jared: smaller precision (4-bit) reduces memory and increases throughput but may have edge-case quality regressions. Redwood Optimize gives recommendations per workload and run evals on your prompt sets to detect regressions automatically. we can run a regression sweep during the pilot.
[00:06:06] Ethan: timeline — we need to present options to exec in two weeks. can you produce a sizing + cost delta by then?
[00:06:12] Maya: yes, we'll aim to have an initial sizing and cost model in 7–10 days.
[00:06:16] Leah: about instrumentation — what telemetry do you provide so we can map user events to token costs and latency?
[00:06:22] Jared: Redwood Console has per-route token and latency breakdown, traces, and sampling hooks. you can attach request IDs to correlate.
[00:06:30] Omar: for the profiling session, we'll need a load generator snippet. do you have an example?
[00:06:35] Jared: yes, i'll share a JMeter/locust example plus a small node script that replays traces. We'll provide a profiling harness that runs at multiple concurrency points and reports p50/p95/p99 and token/sec.
[00:06:47] Leah: good. also curious about how you measure streaming p95 — per-token vs end-to-end?
[00:06:53] Jared: we capture both. streaming p95 per-token measures latency for token emission; end-to-end measures time until final token emitted. For UX, per-token latency matters for first token and smooth streaming.
[00:07:04] Priya: any specifics about multiplexer or scheduling? our app multiplexes many short sessions into few connections to reduce sockets.
[00:07:10] Maya: Redwood supports multiplexing and concurrency limits at router level; we can tune batch windows and max batch sizes per route.
[00:07:18] Ethan: do you support in-flight preemption for emergency low-latency requests?
[00:07:22] Jared: we have priority queuing and fast-lane policies to preempt low-priority batches; works best on Dedicated where you can reserve a fast lane.
[00:07:31] Leah: ok let's talk about pilot: what would a useful pilot look like?
[00:07:34] Maya: suggested pilot — 2-week profiling run: 1) run token/sec traces on Hosted using your sample traces, 2) replicate on Dedicated small reserved pool, 3) test failover routing and per-call policy, 4) run quantization evals on your prompts, and 5) deliver a sizing + cost recommendations doc.
[00:07:51] Omar: for Dedicated, what minimum commit do we need to get predictable latency?
[00:07:55] Maya: depends on model and throughput; often customers reserve small pools (1–3 GPUs) and use autoscale for bursts. we'll recommend based on profiling.
[00:08:03] Priya: any blocker for us to run the profiling on our side? network and KMS won't be in place yet.
[00:08:09] Jared: network isn't required for initial synthetic profiling — we'll run synthetic traces against hosted and a dedicated sandbox. for private deployment we can do later once KMS is provisioned.
[00:08:18] Leah: ok, let's do the profiling. couple of nitty details: can you capture tokenization differences across models? we saw tokens vary for our international text.
[00:08:27] Jared: yes, tokenizer overhead matters. profiling will capture tokenization cost and per-token generation. we'll recommend model variants that are tokenizer-friendly for your languages.
[00:08:35] Ethan: Competitors question: some of our procurement people ask if alternatives like Anthropic/managed OpenAI endpoints would be cheaper for these bursty patterns.
[00:08:44] Maya: cost depends on unit economics and pricing model; some competitors license per-request with no reserved capacity, but Dedicated usually wins for predictable 24/7 workloads. We'll include competitor comparison in the doc.
[00:08:55] Omar: one more question — do you have observability for per-token CPU/GPU breakdown?
[00:09:00] Jared: we expose per-request token counts, queuing time, kernel time estimates. hardware-level counters can be exported for Dedicated.
[00:09:08] Leah: great. anything else from your side?
[00:09:12] Priya: we want to ensure the evals include our 20 prompt archetypes and some adversarial prompts.
[00:09:18] Jared: absolutely. please send the prompt set; we'll run regression checks across quantization and batch settings.
[00:09:24] Maya: recap and immediate next steps — i'll send the benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2 + private whitepaper, and a proposed pilot plan. jared will send the profiling harness. omar to provide anonymized traces.
[00:09:36] Leah: sounds good. timeline: we'll review with execs by 2026-03-19.
[00:09:41] Maya: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email with attachments and calendar invites for the profiling block.
[00:09:48] Ethan: thanks all.
[00:09:50] (call winds down, some crosstalk)

Post-call notes (approx):
- Redwood to run hosted baseline + dedicated sandbox profiling.
- Key constraints: EU residency for certain payloads, SSO + audit logs, p95 ~= 180ms for customer chat, 2k concurrent burst sizing.
- Pilot deliverables: benchmark matrix, profiling harness, sizing + cost doc, quantization regression results.

Transcript imperfections: speaker overlap at 00:09:50, occasional word substitution (we heard "kernel" as "cernel" in auto-transcript), punctuation inconsistent in original export.
